posts.text:
Rather than write about how we’re merging lots of PRs without reading code, I’d prefer to talk about how we’re merging more PRs than we were nine months ago and still reading as much of the code as is conceivably possible.

For all the hot takes, demos, articles and posts out there, we’re still finding mistakes in the code our agents produce, along with some poor architectural decisions. Perhaps we should use the right models, remove their harnesses, trust the deus ex machina. But that’s not what we’re seeing, and I don’t have the resources to run an endless A/B test on feature development to be sure of it.

So let’s talk about how we review all this code without overheating our brains like an overclocked crypto rack.

1. Stacked PRs. It’s easier to read a change when it’s broken into smaller PRs. On our Django backend, for example, we might have one PR for the models, another for the business logic and a third for the API layer.

2. Legible PR descriptions. I’d say we still don’t have this quite right, and our PR-writing skill is still evolving. What helps is a short description of why we’re making the change and a simple flow diagram showing what it does. We also include screenshots and videos from our coding agents so you can see the feature in action.

3. Codiff. Not everyone on the team is using this yet, and I recently forked it to add our own flavour. It’s a review tool that uses an LLM to walk you through a change, breaking it into pieces that tell something of a story. https://lnkd.in/eKs-2fVu

I spent a lot of my first two years at university drawing UML class and sequence diagrams. Rational Rose was the tool of choice. At the time I had no idea why we were doing it, but it was a world of Java and OO design principles. The intention was that you'd end up as a drone in a Java “software factory”, where someone would hand you said diagrams and a set of interfaces and you’d implement your bit. Those diagrams suddenly make a lot more sense now that engineers are finding themselves in weird hybrid roles as systems architects and principal engineers.

When I’m trying to make sense of a 5,000-line PR, I’m reaching back into that world. Each PR now includes a System Overview with component flows, sequence diagrams and call trees showing where the code starts and what it calls next.

The point is to understand your system, what’s being built and why. Without that, entropy creeps in. Some part of the system will break one shiny Sunday night, and you won’t know why or how.

Last week, I had conversations with Estates teams across Health and Education, as well as a number of other sectors. One issue kept coming up: the time it takes to fix things.

It got me thinking about something that hasn't changed, despite the move from Networking and Telecoms into Health Technologies:

Downtime costs organisations far more than just money.

It creates additional pressure, unnecessary delays and, in some cases, risks that simply shouldn't exist.

Think about the knock-on effects:
Delays in bed turnaround times.
Beds and bed spaces taken out of commission.
Alerts taking far longer to reach the right person or people.
Increased operational pressure on already stretched teams.
And, most importantly, additional risks that could potentially be life-threatening.

Much of this is avoidable. The technology, processes and support are there to make things simpler, so why are we still accepting unnecessary delays as the norm?

Getting hands-on with our set up for demonstrations and exhibitions has given me the opportunity to ask plenty of questions and really understand the practical benefits.

The reality is that accidents happen. Components get damaged, connections get pulled and buttons need replacing.

But what if fixing those issues didn't mean waiting days for an engineer?

In under a minute, and at a very low cost, individual modules can be replaced by an Estates or Maintenance team member.

In fact, I can do it myself! It's genuinely that straightforward, and all I need is a small screwdriver.

Of course, just as we see in Networking and Telecoms, IT and Estates teams aren't necessarily expected to diagnose complex software issues. That's where our Ascom support teams come in, providing support through an SLP from the initial call right through to resolution.

But when the issue is a damaged pull cord, a button or a replaceable module, why shouldn't Estates teams be empowered to deal with it themselves?

From the conversations I've had, this simple approach could save organisations 2–3 days in some cases, alongside several hundred pounds in unnecessary costs.

That's a significant difference from what is, in reality, a very simple fix.

We need to start thinking differently about maintenance, downtime and the total cost of ownership.

If you're planning a ward refurbishment, a bed head replacement or a wider healthcare technology refresh, I'd love to have a conversation.

Let's look at how we can reduce costs, minimise downtime, empower your Estates teams and, above all, remove unnecessary risks.

Because ultimately, this isn't just about replacing a module. It's about getting beds back into service quicker, keeping teams working efficiently and helping ensure patients receive the care they need without avoidable disruption.

Are you just asking AI to write emails and generate content?

Or are you actually using it to work like a Developer, QA Engineer, Data Analyst, or Automation Engineer?

As we move towards 2027, the biggest shift is not just AI-powered coding. It's AI-powered execution.

Here are 10 practical ways I'm exploring how AI can transform everyday technical work:

🔍 4. API Testing

- Validate JSON responses.
- Identify negative test cases.
- Automate API regression testing.

📁 5. Documentation

- Create technical documentation.
- Analyse business requirements.
- Generate test plans and test reports.
- Understand unfamiliar codebases.

⚡ 6. AI Agents

- Delegate multi-step tasks to AI.
- Connect AI with external tools.
- Automate repetitive workflows.
- Let agents execute tasks with human supervision.

🧠 7. Learning & Upskilling

- Understand new technologies.
- Practise interview questions.
- Build small projects.
- Learn unfamiliar frameworks faster.

📈 8. Data Analysis

- Analyse Excel and CSV files.
- Generate Python scripts.
- Identify trends and anomalies.
- Create reports and visualisations.

🔐 9. Code Quality & Security

- Identify potential vulnerabilities.
- Review coding standards.
- Analyse dependencies.
- Suggest improvements.

🚀 10. End-to-End Engineering
Imagine giving an AI agent a requirement and having it help with:
Requirement → Code → Unit Testing → API Testing → Database Validation → UI Testing → Documentation.

That's where agentic engineering is heading.

Tools worth exploring:

- Claude & Claude Code
- ChatGPT & Codex

- Gemini
- n8n
- MCP (Model Context Protocol)

🔥 My biggest takeaway:

AI won't make technical knowledge irrelevant.

But professionals who know how to combine domain knowledge, critical thinking, automation, and AI will have a significant advantage.

Don't just learn how to PROMPT AI.

Learn how to BUILD WITH AI, CONNECT AI, and DELEGATE WORK TO AI.

posts.text:
AI can write your code in minutes. But can it figure out why your production system just went down?

I was reading a senior engineer's perspective on the Microsoft outage, and one particular observation made me stop and think.

We often measure AI's capabilities by how quickly it can generate code, build applications, write tests, or even document an entire project.

But are we measuring the right thing?

There's a much bigger layer of software engineering that rarely gets discussed.

Understanding the system.

Think about a production environment.

A single application might depend on:
- Databases
- Infrastructure
- Network configurations
- APIs and integrations
- Multiple interconnected services
- CI/CD pipelines and deployment configurations

Everything works together until one unexpected edge case breaks something.

And suddenly, the challenge isn't writing code anymore.

It's identifying WHERE the failure originated, understanding WHAT it affected, determining WHAT needs to be rolled back, and ensuring that the recovery doesn't create another problem.

This is where experience and system knowledge become critical.

The engineer who has built, maintained, deployed, and troubleshot a system for years has something an AI assistant may not have: deep operational context.

They know the dependencies, the historical decisions, the hidden complexities, and sometimes even the unexpected consequences of a seemingly harmless change.

An engineer unfamiliar with that system might spend hours investigating something that its original developer can identify in minutes.

And this brings me to a thought about the future of software engineering.

AI is becoming exceptionally good at the implementation layer.

But software engineering is much more than implementation.

It's architecture, decision-making, debugging, risk assessment, understanding dependencies, and taking responsibility when things fail.

I don't think the real question is whether AI can replace developers.

I think the more important question is:

Can an engineer who relies entirely on AI without understanding the underlying system safely own a production environment?

Because generating code is one thing.

Understanding its consequences is another.

AI should make engineers more capable, not make engineering judgment optional.

And perhaps the engineers who understand systems deeply will become even more valuable in an AI-driven world.

The future may belong not to those who write the most code, but to those who understand what happens when that code meets reality.

#AI #SoftwareEngineering #DevOps #SystemDesign #ArtificialIntelligence #EngineeringLeadership

posts.text:
Last Thursday, Microsoft 365 went down.

Outlook, Teams, Copilot: out across North America, Europe and Asia-Pacific in one of Microsoft’s longest outages. Companies postponed earnings releases. Government offices ground to a halt.

And then it came back.

That’s the part worth thinking about. Microsoft had the source code, the build pipelines, thousands of engineers and the people who know how it all fits together. Recovery was always going to happen. The only question was when.

Two weeks earlier, a much smaller story played out. Silicon Practice, a GP website supplier, went into administration, affecting potentially hundreds of practices across the UK. NHS England had to write to GPs asking them to work out how to preserve patient information and keep talking to their patients.

Nobody on the other end of that one is working to fix it.

That’s the difference between an outage and a supplier failure. In an outage, the vendor fixes it. When the vendor is gone, all you have is what they left behind, and the question is whether anyone can turn it back into working software.

Most organisations with escrow have never tested that. The deposit sits there: source code, maybe some documentation. 

It rarely includes the build environment, the dependencies, the configuration, or what was in the head of the developer who left three years ago.

At Cleanroom, we take a deposit and rebuild it from scratch in an isolated environment, using only what’s in the deposit. If it builds and runs, you have evidence. If it doesn’t, you find out now, not on the day the administrators are appointed.

So the question this week isn’t “do we have escrow?”

It’s “has anyone ever built from it?”

posts.text:
Before BIM, there was the art of understanding every bar.

Some may call it the old way of preparing Bar Bending Schedules (BBS) using AutoCAD. 

But is it really outdated?

There is something valuable about manually preparing a BBS: you learn to read reinforcement drawings, understand bar shapes, calculate cutting lengths, determine quantities and appreciate how every reinforcement detail comes together.

Today, we have powerful BIM tools like Revit that can automate much of this process. 

But automation should never replace understanding.

The tools may change, but the engineering principles remain the same.

The deeper you understand the fundamentals, the better you become at using advanced tools, interpreting outputs and identifying errors.

At Caitech, we believe in building engineers who understand the concept before relying on the software.

Don't just learn how to generate a BBS. Understand how every number, bar mark and cutting length comes to life.

posts.text:
🚨 ₹39,091.53 spent in just 6 days on an AI subscription. All because of a team invitation.
As a software engineer with 11+ years of experience, I've always appreciated how modern SaaS products simplify collaboration.
But a recent experience with Grok Ultra and its team subscription feature raised a serious question about billing transparency and user trust.
Here's what happened:
📅November 7, 2026
My brother purchased an Ultra subscription for ₹21,012.33, valid until December 7.
📅 November 13, 2026
He invited me to his team, believing we could collaborate using the existing subscription.
Shortly afterward, another ₹18,079.20 was charged to his saved credit card.
💳Total paid: ₹39,091.53
We later learned that each team member requires a separate paid seat.
That's understandable. SaaS companies have every right to charge for additional users.
But here's where the experience becomes concerning.
During the invitation process, we did not notice:
❌ A clear warning about the additional charge.
❌ An obvious pricing breakdown before proceeding.
❌ A separate confirmation explicitly authorizing the additional payment.
Had we clearly understood that inviting another member would trigger an ₹18,000+ charge, we would never have proceeded.
We contacted billing support and explained the situation.
The response?
"We are not able to refund a seat, whether it was purchased by accident or on purpose, and whether it was used or unused."
Our refund request was denied.
But my biggest concern remains unanswered:
Where exactly was the additional payment clearly disclosed and confirmed during the invitation process?
As a frontend engineer, I believe this raises an important product design question.
When a user action can trigger a significant financial transaction, the experience should make three things unmistakably clear:
✅ Price transparency: Show the exact additional cost before the user proceeds.
✅Informed confirmation: Make the financial consequences of the action explicit.
✅Customer trust: Provide a meaningful review process when users report unexpected charges.
A technically functional billing system isn't necessarily a good user experience.
Good UX isn't just about reducing friction. It's about preventing expensive misunderstandings.
We're not asking for free access.
We're asking for transparency, a fair review, and an explanation of how this additional purchase was authorized.
I genuinely value AI tools like Grok and Cursor, but experiences like this can affect customer confidence.
I'd appreciate a response from the teams involved.
To fellow developers, UX designers, SaaS founders and product leaders:
Should adding a teammate to a paid SaaS subscription require a separate, clearly visible confirmation of the additional charge?
I'd love to hear your thoughts.

𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲’𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗻𝘂𝗺𝗯𝗲𝗿 𝗜’𝗱 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝘂𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝗻𝘆. 
It’s almost never in the deck.

Not revenue. Not pipeline. Not ARR. Not how accurate the model is.
What did the second deployment cost, compared to the first?

If the second one cost nearly as much as the first - new integration, new data wrangling, another six months of engineers on a plane, then it isn’t a product company. It’s a consultancy with very good branding. That can be a fine business. It just doesn't deserve as software multiple, and anyone looking closely works that out eventually.

If the second cost a fraction of the first, something else is going on. The learning is being captured somewhere it can be reused, and every site makes the next one cheaper and more certain.

But here’s what that ratio is really measuring, and it isn’t engineering. It’s proof.

In this sector the asset being built isn’t software. It’s evidence - the accumulated record of having worked somewhere that mattered, in front of people with something to lose. Models commoditise. Chips commoditise. Capital is abundant and getting cheaper. Evidence doesn’t transfer, and it can’t be bought.

Which is why whoever gets there first will be hard to catch. Not because the technology gap will be wide but because the one behind has to spend real time inside other people’s operations - and you cannot buy your way past somebody else’s shutdown schedule.

So the scarce thing isn’t money or talent. It’s reaching deployment two, three and four quickly, somewhere hard enough that the learning is worth having. Reselling somebody else’s stack won’t get you there. The margin gets squeezed and you own none of the learning.

Today the market prices models.

I think it will price deployment queues - who has access to the hard places, and how fast they can get through them.

Which makes this region more interesting than it’s usually read as being. Hard environments, concentrated ownership, decisions taken in weeks.

Don’t ask what the model can do.
Ask what the second one costs.

posts.text:
A lot of businesses around the world will be discussing how to make their systems more resilient today, and that’s mainly thanks to the Microsoft outage on Friday. Turns out having all your eggs in one basket is a bad business strategy.

I believe there are only three solutions to this problem right now. Diversify your services, for example don’t get all your communications services from one provider (email, video calls, etc). Move stuff off the cloud, for example you don’t need office products in the cloud (document editor, spreadsheet, etc). Have backup services when primary services go down, that includes data storage.

I’d recommend getting a move on when implementing safeguards. I strongly believe there will be more of these issues going forward, I also think they will become much worse in terms of severity. Being blunt about it, this is due to the impact of AI. A lot of the cloud providers are cutting their experienced staff because of AI, and a lot of code is being generated and not properly reviewed because of AI. No company will want to admit AI is to blame, as that’s the golden goose after all. I’m not criticising AI as a technology, but many of these SaaS platforms are rushing these changes, when they are critical infrastructure providers, and should be the slowest to adopt, not the fastest.

SaaS platforms have also deliberately built their products to work entirely in the cloud when they don’t have to. Legacy software providers have stopped supporting desktop products and forced customers onto modern cloud-based alternatives, simply because making you rent a product generates more recurring revenue. Here is the kicker: SaaS products can be designed to work offline too, and that applies to both web and mobile applications. The reason they aren’t comes down purely to cost and control. SaaS companies don’t want to build software that is more expensive to engineer, and they want complete control over access to their products.

So as a customer, you end up paying more for far less resilience!

posts.text:
If Humans Cannot Read the Code, What Must They See Before Merging the PR?
AI can turn human intent into specifications, code, tests, and pull requests.
But after the tests finish, who turns the technical results back into evidence that a human can actually understand?
If the final report is still a collection of coverage percentages, status codes, latency measurements, and green “Passed” labels, we have not achieved No-Code.
The human has simply moved from being unable to read the code to being unable to read the test report.
Assume the final decision remains human. The person deciding whether to merge cannot review the code.
The problem is not who has the authority. It is whether that person has enough evidence to make a responsible decision.
“42 tests passed.”
“Unit test coverage reached 87%.”
“The endpoint returned HTTP 200.”
These may be useful technical results. Even in plain English, they do not tell a non-engineer:
whether the requested user outcome was achieved;
which real actions and scenarios were verified;
how the actual result compared with the expected result;
which failure paths remain untested; or
what risks the available tests cannot exclude.
Human-readable Evidence is not a simplified test report. It must reconstruct the relationship between human intent, expected behavior, actual behavior, and remaining uncertainty.
Instead of reporting only:
Checkout E2E test passed.
The evidence might say:
A customer added two products to the cart, applied a discount code, and paid by credit card.
The order total changed from NT1,200toNT1,200toNT1,080. Payment succeeded, the order was created, inventory was reduced, and the customer received a confirmation.
Interrupted payment, duplicate payment, and insufficient inventory were not verified.
Now the human can compare:
What I expected the system to do
with
What the system actually did—and did not verify.
This is not merely test-report summarization. It is Evidence Reconstruction.
The development process transforms human intent into forms a machine can execute:
Human Intent → Specification → Code → Test Execution
The verification process must return in the opposite direction:
Technical Results → Human-readable Evidence → Human Judgment
Without that return path, No-Code hides the implementation but does not make software quality understandable.
Even perfect evidence cannot help if the specification misunderstood the original intent. That hidden gap between Vibe Coding and SDD is the subject of my next relay.
True No-Code should not require a human to become a software engineer before they can judge whether the result is correct.
If you could not read the code and had access only to the Specification, Acceptance Criteria, and Test Evidence, what would the AI have to show you before you were willing to merge the pull request?

• 1M Token Context & Output Window: Features a 1,048,576 unified context window with up to 1M output tokens via background long decode.

• Developer-Friendly Pricing: Flat rate of \$1.50 per 1M input tokens and \$7.50 per 1M output tokens.
• Multi-File Debugging & Parallel Tooling: Native batching of file-read and search calls to discover and repair root-cause bugs across repositories without rewriting unrelated files.
• Benchmark Performance: Leads its class with 13.5% on SWE-sweep, 58.8% on HLE-Diamond, 71.6% on Agents' Last Exam v1.1, and 76.1% on AutomationBench-AA.

posts.text:
Spend your time designing the parts of a system that are expensive to change. Leave the rest to evolve.

Early in my career I saw a team spend 6 months designing every class, every method, and every interaction before writing any code.  At the time I suppose it felt rigorous, obviously it wasn't.  The design was wrong almost the second the moment it met reality. Not totally wrong but wrong enough to make the effort impossible to justify.

We have obviously moved on but I still see echoes of it today:

“My class has an external interface so we need to design it.”

Even when the person consuming that interface is sitting across the desk.  IMO, here’s the distinction that actually matters, it's not internal vs external (or whatever). It's

What is cheap to change vs what is expensive to change.

Two software engineers, working closely, can sketch an interface, build it, break it, and refine it in a few hours. So in that context it’s just an unnecessary constraint. But if we change the context: different teams, time zones, companies, long-lived APIs, defined protocols or hardware constraints then the same interface can become expensive. In the latter case we're no longer just designing code, we’re designing an agreement and that's where design effort matters.

I also think there’s another dimension to this. Not just what is expensive to change but also what is likely to change.

If something is likely to change, think about how easily it can change.

This doesn't mean predicting every future requirement or building abstractions for possibilities that may never happen.  It means avoiding decisions that make an expected change unnecessarily difficult. We can sum this up as:

If it's expensive to change, design it carefully.
If it's likely to change, and changing it isn't trivial, design it so it can evolve.

These ideas are related but they're not quite the same thing. So what’s actually worth designing?
- Architectural boundaries
- Key abstractions
- Persistent data
- Cross organisational Interfaces
- Things that are costly or hard to observe

Everything else? I'd suggest just figuring it out in the code.

A useful rule of thumb:

Design until the cost of not deciding exceeds the cost of being wrong.

If it’s cheap to change, it’s probably too early to decide.  That said I'll add one important caveat: 

“Don’t over-design” does not mean “don’t think”.

Before writing code I still expect engineers, especially junior ones, to explain how they think things will hold together. Not in minute detail but enough to show the intended solution's shape. I've found it's better to discover the mess early than own it later.

To my mind it's about solving the right problems in the right way and at a time when they matter.

Your website might look brilliant to a human visitor, yet remain completely invisible to the way customers actually search today.

Last month, I sat down with a UK consultancy founder whose inbound enquiries had quietly dipped over the past year, despite having a sleek, modern website.

When we typed the exact questions their ideal clients ask into ChatGPT, Perplexity, and Google’s AI Overviews, their company wasn't mentioned once. Instead, competitors with far simpler websites were being recommended by name.

The rules of online discovery have shifted beneath our feet. People no longer want to scroll through 10 blue links and piece together research themselves; they ask an AI assistant for a direct answer and trust the 2 or 3 sources it cites.

Traditional websites built around vague marketing slogans and buried service details give answer engines nothing concrete to latch onto. If a machine cannot cleanly parse who you are, what problem you solve, and why you are credible, it simply skips past you.

If you want your digital foundations built for Answer Engine Optimisation (AEO), start with three practical shifts:
✅ Lead with direct, answer-first clarity: Structure your core service pages around the real questions customers ask, placing clear, factual answers right at the top rather than hiding them behind clever taglines.
✅ Keep your entity details consistent everywhere: Ensure your company name, services, location, and credentials match word-for-word across your website, LinkedIn, Companies House records, and directories so AI models trust your authority.
✅ Add structured schema markup under the bonnet: Implementing clean JSON-LD schema (such as Organisation, Service, and FAQ markup) acts like a well-labelled technical index, helping answer engines read your site without guesswork.

Strong digital foundations aren't about chasing every passing algorithm tweak; they are about making your real-world expertise unmistakable to both humans and machines.

Have you tried asking ChatGPT or Perplexity who the best provider in your sector is locally? Did your business make the list?

posts.text:
Engineering software is becoming easier to replicate. CAD included.

Over the past few weeks, I have seen several YouTube videos declaring the end of commercial CAD. The trigger: SolidCraft, a free, open-source CAD application available in the browser and on desktop. Naturally, it comes with an MCP server so AI agents can create and modify models directly.

I tested it with Grok 4.7 and created a simple component.

My assessment: intuitive, easy to use, and useful for basic modeling. Also: limited functionality and some clear constraints. For a private 3D-printing project at home, I can see the appeal. Based on my test, I would not consider it a replacement for an established commercial CAD system.

Still, seeing a tool like this emerge so quickly should make engineering software vendors pay attention.

At the same time, “Reverse Engineer Anything” has attracted more than 460,000 GitHub stars. It connects agents to tools that inspect existing applications, investigate how features work, and help build new implementations (thanks to Charlie Hills for the visualization).

We have spent this year building our own applications through vibe coding. Now, existing software increasingly provides the reference for what to build and how it should behave.
That puts pressure on the economics of software development. Although reproducing selected functionality is still a long way from matching an entire engineering system.

In CAD, the difficult parts include robust geometry operations, predictable model regeneration, large assemblies, and preserving design intent when exchanging data. Years of handling unusual customer models matter.

But the direction is becoming harder to ignore.

As software becomes easier to reproduce, vendors will have to justify more of their value through dependable operation.

Features and interfaces will face growing competition. Maintenance, compatibility, integration, and credible service-level commitments will carry more weight in purchasing decisions.

Companies will continue paying for software they can deploy reliably, support over years, and trust with their engineering workflows. Someone needs to take responsibility when an update breaks a model or an interface stops working.

Switching will become easier in some parts of the toolchain. In others, decades of product data and process dependencies will remain a substantial barrier.

My expectation: more engineering software will become commodity, while reliable industrial operation remains a business worth paying for.

posts.text:
The day rate is the wrong number to compare hiring models on (Europe tech team series, part 1)

Most founders compare hiring models on the wrong number.
They put a salary next to a day rate next to an agency quote, and pick the smallest.

The smallest number is rarely the cheapest team.
Ravio puts the median UK mid-level software engineer at £74,000. That's the salary, not the cost. Add employer contributions, recruitment fees, management time and the months before they're shipping useful code.
Cross a border and it moves again. Employer charges can reach 40–45% of gross salary in France, against roughly 20–23% in Germany and around 22% in Poland. An employer of record adds a platform fee on top: published prices run from $199 to $699 per person per month.

A UK contractor looks expensive at a median of £550 a day (IT Jobs Watch). But there are no employer overheads, and you can stop when the work stops.
So which is cheapest? It depends on how long you need the work, and on what happens when it goes wrong.
That second part usually gets skipped.

Every hiring model puts the risk somewhere.

A permanent hire puts it on you: a bad hire is yours to fix. A contractor raises the question of whether they're really working like an employee. An employer of record means trusting someone else's local compliance, including who owns the code. An outsourced partner keeps the knowledge on their side of the fence. Augmented engineers sit in your codebase every day, which works well until the engagement ends and nobody wrote anything down.
None of these is a reason to rule a model out. They're reasons to price it properly.

So compare four things, not one:
 Cost over the whole period you need the work.
 Time until someone is shipping useful code.
 Where the risk sits, and who carries it.
 How much knowledge stays with you when it ends.

Most software engineers treat the OS kernel and hardware as clean abstractions. But on bare-metal silicon like the liquid-cooled Intel Xeon Platinum 8480\+ \(112 cores, 4 NUMA nodes, 1TB RAM, 100GbE ConnectX-7\), physical hardware boundaries dictate your real throughput.

Consider what actually happens under heavy load with Memory ordering semantics: std::memory\_order\_seq\_cst vs acquire-release.

When systems rely on default sequentially consistent atomics \(seq\_cst\) on all shared operations, the underlying hardware behaves in ways standard computer science textbooks rarely discuss.

The Root Cause at the Silicon Level:
Sequential consistency imposes a strict global memory ordering across all cores, requiring expensive hardware memory barriers \(mfence on x86, dmb on ARM\) that stall store buffers.

The Telemetry Comparison \(100k Concurrent Load\):
- Baseline \(default sequentially consistent atomics \(seq\_cst\) on all shared operations\): CPU store buffers forced to flush globally, dragging queue throughput down
- Tuned \(fine-grained acquire-release semantics \(memory\_order\_acquire / release\)\): 2.8x higher message throughput on lock-free single-producer single-consumer queues

The Production Action Plan:
Use memory\_order\_release on writes and memory\_order\_acquire on reads when synchronizing state transitions, reserving seq\_cst only for global total-order consensus algorithms.

Key Takeaway: High throughput is rarely just an algorithmic challenge in modern low-latency systems. It is almost always a cache coherence, memory bus arbitration, or kernel synchronization bottleneck.

posts.text:
Decision making is now the bottleneck. Frankly it has always been, but bigger companies had too much risk accumulated to see it clearly.

When developers used to spend sprints on simple features it wasn't because they couldn't move faster, it was because they had to make a lot of decisions favoring derisking the business in the environment where code was written by humans, read and understood by humans, changed and extended by humans.

This accumulated risk was the reason why small startups could launch and torpedo existing companies in a matter of weeks, then get a major injection and dominate a category in a year and then seemingly just stop evolving and freeze up, repainting buttons and micro optimizing every piece of the flow.

Now the environment is different. Engineering task right now is twofold - enable code-to-production data pipeline and facilitate quick turnaround and feedback loops with the customer and business stakeholders.

The code to production data pipeline is a fundamental change in how the profession is changing. Now we are not crafting software, now we are enabling a smooth continuous well controlled flow of changes of our software. Think multi pass stages of code refinement, normalization, verification, deduplication etc etc. Once you see the similarities to the data world - you can't unsee it. 

This is the new Platform Engineering job, this is where all the accrued expertise is going to go, all the tech minded engineers who are in it to kill a dragon or solve a puzzle.

On the other end of the spectrum you have the Product Engineering job. It attracts the soft skill maxxing engineers, with deep empathy for the customer and for the business and a flexible, agile wit.

So far I don't see other solidifying roles in the new world, but if I am missing those - let me know. It's a field that is constantly evolving in which you have to fly a rocket in order to stand still.

posts.text:
35,000 apps built with AI were open to anyone on the internet.

Nobody hacked them.

They were public by default.

Security firm Claroc tested apps made with Grok's AI app builder.

Of 37,571 live apps, 35,578 could be opened without signing in.

That's almost 95%.

Most were harmless.

But an estimated 650 to 800 contained private business or personal data.

Some reportedly included patient records, internal sales data and passwords.

Even 24 apps built by the company's own staff were exposed.

Here's why I think this is interesting.

The problem wasn't a clever attack.

It was a setting.

When people published their apps, the sharing option was already set to "Anyone with the link."

Most people never changed it.

And app addresses aren't as secret as people assume.

Researchers say they can show up in publicly available internet records.

Think about who uses AI app builders.

Not just engineers.

Marketers.

Sales teams.

Founders.

Operations people building a quick tool for their team.

They describe what they want.

The AI builds it.

They click publish.

Done in minutes.

That speed is the whole point.

But nobody asked:

Who can see this?

But there's a catch.

This isn't only a Grok problem.

Researchers point out similar exposure issues with other AI app builders and share features.

And at least one major builder already sets new apps to private by default.

So this isn't "AI app builders are unsafe."

It's that defaults decide what millions of non-technical users actually do.

Still, I think it's one of the clearest lessons of the vibe-coding era.

AI made building software easy.

It didn't make building it safely automatic.

The faster we build, the more important it becomes to ask one boring question before clicking publish:

Who can see this?

#AI #Cybersecurity #NoCode #Business

posts.text:
A few years ago, I sat with a founder who had just proven her idea in a university lab. The physics worked. The early results beat imported alternatives. Then her grant ran out, and every investor she met said, “Come back when you have a prototype and a pilot.” But building that prototype was exactly what she needed funding for.
 
That’s the valley of death for Indian deeptech: TRL 3 to 5, the stretch between proving a concept in the lab and having a working prototype in the real world.
 
India doesn’t lack ideas. Nasscom counts over 3,600 deeptech startups in the country. But very few make it across.
 
For every 100 Indian deep tech companies that raise a seed round, only 23 go on to raise a Series A or B, and just 1 reaches late stage. Globally, those numbers are 105 and 26. In other words, roughly three in four Indian deeptech startups never raise a second round, and 99 in 100 never reach scale.

Why is this stage so hard to fund?

→ It falls between two worlds. Grants stop once the research is done. Most VCs wait for pilots and revenue. TRL 3 to 5 belongs to neither.
 →It’s slow and capital-hungry. Building a working prototype takes labs, specialised equipment and certification, with more time and money than software.
 →It needs more than money. Founders need a lab to build in, tools to test with, the first engineers to hire, and an early customer to shape the product. Most of that is locked inside universities, research institutions and large industry.
 →India’s capital is thinner here. Deeptech gets 7% of Indian VC dollars, against 16% globally, and the average Indian deeptech seed round is $1.3M against $5.8M globally.

Why back companies at this stage? Because it’s where the outcome is decided. Whether a technology becomes a company is settled between TRL 3 and 5, and the right capital and support here change the odds more than at any later stage.
 
That’s why we built Akti. We back founders at TRL 3 to 5 in semiconductors, space and defence, robotics and advanced manufacturing, and clean energy, and stay with them until they reach their first customers.
 
Every week, we’ll share what we’re seeing in these spaces. If you’re building at this stage, we’d love to hear from you:deals@aktiventures.in

Data: Nasscom; Speciale Invest, India’s Deep Tech Revolution (2026), Tracxn.

posts.text:
Every weekday at 12:15, Nikola's father rang the bell, took the pram and left.

"You work. I walk," Branko said, and that was the whole conversation.

Mila was six weeks old when it started. Nikola was thirty-two, a software engineer working from the spare room. He had promised himself he would be the father his own father never had time to be.

Now his father was taking the one hour of the day Nikola could have spent with her.

He said nothing for three weeks. He just watched from the window with cold coffee in his hand. A man who had never pushed a pram in his life turned the corner without looking back.

On Thursday, Nikola muted a planning call and followed them.

He found them in the park. Branko was walking the long loop slowly, stopping at every bench with both hands on the handle and breathing hard. Then he straightened up and went again.

"Dad. If it's too much, give her to me."

Branko didn't answer. He sat down, took out his wallet and unfolded something soft with age.

It was a child's drawing in green crayon. A small stick figure running. A big one far behind. Underneath, in a five-year-old's capitals: DAD SLOW.

"You gave me this on your birthday," Branko said. "Thirty years at a desk. By the time you could run, I could not follow you to the gate."

He folded it again, carefully.

"I am not going to be behind her too."

Nikola sat down beside him and thought about his own days. Eleven hours in the chair. Lunch at the keyboard. Stiff legs on the stairs at night, which he had blamed on the baby.

Nobody chooses to fall behind. It happens one comfortable afternoon at a time, so quietly that a child notices before you do.

And it reverses the same way. A walk after lunch. Ten minutes, then twenty. The stairs instead of the lift. Nothing heroic, just repeated until it becomes your day.

The next day at 12:15, Nikola closed his laptop before the bell rang.

Branko looked down at his son's trainers and said nothing. He just moved over and left half the handle free.

Some fathers spend thirty years catching up. Nikola started before his daughter could crawl.

Coach Sanoob, founder of SanoobFit

posts.text:
In Indonesia, shopping spikes follow content, not just calendars. The Ministry of Trade reported that during Harbolnas 2025, 54% of consumers shopped through creator affiliate links and 80% used livestream features.

On Tokopedia and TikTok Shop’s 10.10 promo this year, transactions rose 9x and 4x respectively, according to the platforms.

For anyone running an online store, that changes how you plan for peak days:

• A spike can start in seconds, when a creator goes live or a flash sale opens, not on a schedule

• It doesn’t peak once. It peaks in waves, all day

• The checkout page takes the hit, not the product page

Three things that help:

1. Scale on demand, not on a timetable: auto-scaling that reacts in minutes, and is tested before the day
2. Protect checkout: queues and rate limits, so a wave slows people down instead of breaking things
3. Cache what you can: product pages, images and search results, ahead of the spike

If a creator sold out 10,000 units in ten minutes, what would happen to your checkout?

On 6 and 7 November 2026, we hosted the LLMNetOps Main Workshop in Malang.

40 network engineers and IT professionals from 24 institutions across Indonesia, from Aceh to Ambon, joined us for two days of hands-on activities.

The workshop focused on a practical question: how can campus network teams use locally deployed AI to support their daily work without giving up control of their systems and data?

- On the first day, participants discussed operational challenges, set up a virtual network lab, and installed the LLMNetOps stack alongside an open-weight LLM that could run on their own laptops.

- On the second day, participants used the virtual network lab, which represented a campus network, to work through two simulated network incidents with LLMNetOps. They also explored potential applications in cybersecurity and other campus operations.

LLMNetOps is a self-hosted AI co-pilot for network operations. An engineer can describe an issue in natural language, such as "Users in Building A cannot get an IP address. Check the router." The agent can inspect authorized devices, gather diagnostic information, and present findings for the operator to review. It is designed to run on institutional infrastructure, so sensitive network data can remain under the institution's control.

A principle behind this work is that engineers remain responsible for operational decisions. LLMNetOps is intended to help them investigate problems and handle routine tasks, especially when campus IT teams are working with limited staff and growing demands.

Before the main workshop, we piloted the materials with three institutions in Malang. Their feedback helped us improve the exercises. It was rewarding to see participants, including some with no previous AI experience, deploy and use the platform themselves.

My thanks to Widy Widyawan from Universitas Gadjah Mada for representing IDREN; to my fellow speakers and the development team fromUniversity of Brawijaya IT; theFaculty of Computer Science (FILKOM) University of Brawijaya; to the organizing committee and our three pilot institutions; and to everyone who participated.

This project is supported by a grant from the APNIC Foundation through ISIF Asia 2025 fund.

Participants are now preparing to bring what they learned back to their institutions. We will continue with online follow-up workshops as they begin deployment. We are also progressively releasing LLMNetOps components and supporting materials as open-source software on GitHub.

As a UI/UX designer, I never thought I would end up making a game 🎮

This was my very first Game Jam at Apple Developer Academy @ UC, Jakarta. My team and I built When The Light Is Out, a side-scrolling survival horror game set inside a commuter train. The rule is simple: move when the lights are on, stop when they go out. Something is waiting in the dark. 

I worked on the ideation and the art. I drew all the visual assets in Procreate, which I had never opened before this project. I'm used to grids and clean interfaces, so drawing characters and backgrounds by hand felt strange at first. I had to learn it fast, while the deadline kept getting closer.

It ended up being one of the most fun things I've done here. I found out I really enjoy illustrating, and that game design asks the same question I ask in UI/UX every day: how will this feel for the person using it? This time, the answer we wanted was fear.

I also worked closely with the developers, adjusting my drawings quickly so they could keep building. 

Thank you to my team for making this such a good memory. 💜

# 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗜 𝗪𝗔𝗥 𝗠𝗔𝗬 𝗡𝗢𝗧 𝗕𝗘 𝗪𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚𝗚𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗚𝗣𝗨. 𝗜𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗬 𝗕𝗘 𝗪𝗢𝗡 𝗕𝗬 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡.

Was the Jensen Huang–NVIDIA crisis a Chinese pre-emptive strike on America's AI industry?

It is a provocative thesis, not an established fact. US reporting describes an investigation into Alice Huang's alleged links to Chinese intelligence; the allegations remain unproven and Beijing denies them. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair and Reuters reported his resignation as NVIDIA CEO on November 12. But no public evidence proves Beijing orchestrated the affair or engineered a US AI financing crisis.

Still, the strategic vulnerability deserves attention.

NVIDIA became more than a chip supplier. It sits at the intersection of GPUs, AI-cloud customers, strategic investments and data-centre finance. GPUs can support asset-backed lending; NVIDIA investments can help customers expand capacity—and buy more NVIDIA hardware.

That is not automatically fraud. The risk is concentration: if confidence, collateral values and customer funding weaken together, the network can transmit the shock.

But the bigger shift may matter more than the scandal.

AI is moving from one-size-fits-all closed models towards specialised services. Think of the Windows era: a common platform enabled thousands of applications for accounting, banking, insurance and manufacturing. Open-weight models could do the same for AI.

Developers need not train frontier models. They can adapt existing models, connect company data and build applications for claims, credit, tax, reconciliation, fraud detection and investment research.

𝗡𝗼𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝘀𝗸 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗻 𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗜𝗔 𝗚𝗣𝗨.

Frontier training and heavy inference still need powerful accelerators. But document processing, rules engines, orchestration and smaller-model inference can often run economically on CPUs. The future is heterogeneous computing—not GPU-or-nothing.

Palantir illustrates the application layer: connecting models to enterprise data and real workflows. It has not replaced NVIDIA with its own chips; its AI partnerships also include NVIDIA. Application software may capture enormous value.

The economic disruption:

• Intelligence becomes cheaper.  
• Industry expertise becomes more valuable.  
• Smaller firms can build specialized AI products.  
• Productivity spreads beyond hyperscalers.  
• Hardware choices become more diverse.

China's open-weight ecosystem could benefit—but so can developers everywhere, including Indonesia.

The contest may not be whose model is smartest. It may be who embeds useful, affordable AI into millions of organizations.

NVIDIA helped build the engine room of the AI boom. The next wave may belong to application builders.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗚𝗣𝗨 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘄𝗮𝘆. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝘆 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝗳𝗳 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗶𝘁.

posts.text:
What gives visitors a reason to return after opening day?
For a resort or cultural tourism destination in Southeast Asia, that question belongs in the first design brief. AOTO NEXUS uses the AOTO 6E Experience Value Framework to connect site planning, visitor experience design, project delivery and ongoing operations.
1. Explore — Understand the site, its cultural and natural assets, the people you want to attract, and what your team can build and operate.
2. Extract — Choose a theme visitors can understand and remember. Test whether it can support activities, spaces and future programming.
3. Experience — Map the visit from arrival to departure. Where will guests stop, take part, rest, spend and share what they did?
4. Express — Give the theme a physical form through landscape, architecture, wayfinding and activities people can join.
5. Execute — Check that the design fits the budget, can be built with the available materials and trades, and can be maintained by the operator.
6. Evolve — Use visitor feedback, seasonal events and refreshed activities to give people a reason to come back.
Imagine a riverside resort in Indonesia working with local batik makers. A short route from reception to a shaded workshop can make the craft part of the visit. Before construction, check access, rain protection and staffing. After opening, the operator can use guest feedback to refine the workshop and try a seasonal craft market.
If you’re planning or renewing a leisure destination, start with one question: What should guests be able to do here that they’ll remember and want to do again?
AOTO NEXUS supports leisure developers with cultural tourism planning, landscape design and owner advisory through delivery. https://aotonexus.com/

An interesting update from Indonesia this week.

According to recent reports citing PLN Batam, electricity currently supplied to the island's data center sector remains below 50 MW, with fewer than 10 companies having signed power purchase agreements.

Meanwhile, Batam continues to attract significant interest in data center investment.

This highlights an important distinction:

Announced capacity ≠ Operational capacity.

For data center developers, securing electricity is only part of the challenge.

Reliable UPS systems, redundancy planning, power distribution, and cooling infrastructure are equally important when turning a project into an operational facility.

At ACwatt, we focus on UPS and critical power protection solutions that support this infrastructure.

Indonesia's digital infrastructure story is still developing, and Batam is certainly a market worth watching.

This month Jensen left Nvidia. Also this month, I left Greentic. Different reasons, I promise. Slightly smaller headlines too

For the last 8 months I led research engineering at Greentic. We built an AI agent platform in Rust, pretty much from zero. Agents run inside WASM, use tools through MCP, talk to 23 LLM providers, and every token gets billed to the right tenant. The same platform deploys to Azure AKS, Cloud Run, Kubernetes, AWS ECS or a regular VM, even with no internet

The hardest part was keeping the agents working after every change. An agent can look perfect in a demo and give a wrong answer a week later, so I spent a lot of time on testing with LLM judges, replaying old conversations, and building an audit view in production that shows where conversations break and how much they cost

Unlike Jensen, I cannot afford a long break, so I am looking for my next job. Full time or contract, remote, any stack is fine (Rust is my favorite). Based in Indonesia, GMT+7

An idea is exciting. Getting it into production is where things get interesting. 🚀
Almost everyone has ideas for a new platform, SaaS product, marketplace, or eCommerce business.
But turning that idea into reliable software requires more than a good-looking interface.
You need someone who can understand the bigger picture.
Someone who can think about frontend architecture, backend services, APIs, integrations, databases, performance, and what happens when real users start using the product.
That's the side of engineering I genuinely enjoy.

One thing I've learned along the way:
Writing code is only part of the job. Understanding what you're building and why it matters is just as important.
I enjoy taking ownership, collaborating with different teams, asking questions before making assumptions, and finding practical solutions instead of introducing unnecessary complexity.
And occasionally, explaining why a feature that sounds like a five-minute task needs a little more than five minutes. 😄

posts.text:
Every senior expert was once allowed to be bad at the job while learning it.
Picture a nineteen year old, fresh out of school, applying to answer calls, help in an office, or write simple code.
Australia's central bank looked at exactly those doors this week. In a paper on November 9, Reserve Bank economist Mike Major tracked where AI pressure shows up first: jobs whose tasks look closest to what AI already does, and the youngest people trying to enter them.
Postings have fallen since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. The steepest fall sits with general clerks, programmers, business analysts, call centre workers and receptionists.
Inside that group, workers aged 15 to 24 have weaker employment, higher unemployment and the clearest drop in hours. In less exposed jobs, that age gap does not appear.
The bank keeps the nuance. Three quarters of firms said AI changed nothing about headcount. About 12 percent are slowing hiring or leaving roles unfilled. Exposure measures resemblance. It does not prove cause for every missing posting.
One detail stayed with me. The share of firms using no AI at all fell from about a third in 2025 to nearly zero in 2026.
A company rarely announces this. It simply leaves a junior role unposted. Training is a brand asset. Firms that keep hiring young people, with AI as tutor, build the team others will wish they had kept.
Second signal, a lab that disappeared into the model itself.
OpenAI has dissolved its standalone robotics team for the second time, moving researchers into its core and applied teams. It frames this as speeding robotics up. Its general models, including GPT-6 Astra, can apparently control robots directly.
Safer ground for a business sits with customers, distribution, physical presence and trust. Ground a model release cannot copy overnight.
Third signal, far from the usual chips.
Meituan, the Chinese delivery group, released LongCat 2.5 as open weights. Anyone can download and run it. It has 1.6 trillion parameters, was built for agents, and scores 88.4 on Terminal Bench, just behind Claude Opus 5.
Training used Chinese hardware entirely, according to the reporting. The sample runs on 194 Huawei Ascend chips, with no Nvidia mention. A parallel stack now exists.
If the model keeps absorbing the work around it, what are you keeping that it cannot absorb?

**My Recent Recruitment Experience with Infosys – A Request for Transparency and Better Candidate Communication**

I would like to share my recent recruitment experience with **Infosys**.

I participated in multiple rounds of interviews for a Java Full Stack Developer opportunity, including technical, managerial, and Angular (secondary skill) discussions.

Throughout the process, I invested considerable time and effort in preparing for each round and was genuinely excited about the opportunity to become part of Infosys.

Following the interview discussions, I was informed that my application was being considered for further processing. However, after waiting for an update, I was eventually informed by the Talent Acquisition team that the position was temporarily on hold.

Later, after raising a request through the official Talent Assist channel, I received confirmation that my candidature could not be considered for the current set of requirements.

I completely understand that business requirements, hiring priorities, and organizational decisions can change. However, as a candidate who has invested significant time and effort across multiple interview rounds, I believe timely communication and constructive feedback would make a meaningful difference.

**A few suggestions for improving the candidate experience:**
- Maintain transparent communication throughout the recruitment process.
- Provide timely updates regarding application status.
- Share constructive feedback whenever possible.
- Ensure candidates receive clear closure after completing multiple interview rounds.

I still respect Infosys as an organization and hope this feedback will be taken positively.

I believe a positive candidate experience is just as important as the recruitment process itself.

**Hoping the Infosys Talent Acquisition team considers this feedback constructively.**
